newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Austria economy seen picking up, on track for EMU.
newsitem.headline: Austria economy seen picking up, on track for EMU.

text.p: Austrian economists on Thursday raised their 1997 growth forecasts for the economy and said they were confident the country was on course to join the European economic and monetary union (EMU) in 1999.
But they warned that a high current account deficit could pose a major economic problem.

Vienna's WIFO research institute, whose figures form the basis of government policy, raised its gross domestic product growth forecast 1997 to 1.2 percent from 1.0 percent earlier and its 1996 estimate to 0.8 percent from 0.7.

The move follows an upgrade on Wednesday by the Paris-based Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD), which revised its 1996 GDP growth forecast to 1.1 percent from 0.8 percent in June. It predicts 1.4 percent growth in 1997.
WIFO expects the pick-up to accelerate in 1998, with growth reaching 2.2 percent, based on expectations of strong exports and investments.
"The positive message is that we know definitely that the business cycle interrupted in 1995 is now continuing," WIFO board member Karl Aiginger told a news conference.

"Moreover, the budget is on course for the Maastricht treaty. We expect the deficit criteria will be fulfilled by the Austrian economy," he continued. Countries joining the launch of EMU in January 1999 must reduce their budget deficit to GDP ratio to no more than three percent. But Aiginger said Austria's economic growth still lagged behind the European average of 2.0 percent, due mainly to weak demand from key trading partners Germany, Italy and Switzerland.
"The bad news is that our current account balance is still negative for the third year in a row," he said.
"Let's not forget it's a creeping growth, better than nothing but not spectacular," agreed Bernhard Felderer, chief economist at Vienna's Institute for Advanced Studies.
WIFO saw foreign demand boosted by improved competitiveness resulting from greater currency stability in preparation for EMU, strong industrial productivity growth and restrained wage policies.
"Export demand and investment is good, but internal demand is weak, especially in construction," said WIFO researcher Markus Marterbauer.
The WIFO raised its current account deficit forecast for 1997 to 44 billion schillings from 25.8 billion and for 1996 to 47 billion schillings from its previous estimate of 44.4 billion.
"The high current account deficit threatens to become a major economic problem," WIFO noted in a report.

But, Marterbauer said consumers had cut savings instead of curbing consumption, and businesses had increased their investments by 20 percent in 1996, reflecting confidence in the government's austerity measures.
"We expect to see an upswing in private consumption in 1998 when the (budget) consolidation package is over," he said.
WIFO sees inflation at 1.9 percent for 1997, a slight rise from previous estimates of 1.7, buoyed by a rise in crude oil prices, and expects it to fall only in 1998 to 1.6 percent.
